one_liner: Maintained zlib fork with SIMD deflate, inflate and CRC32/Adler32; about 2.2-2.5x faster compression and 1.5x faster decompression than zlib.
what_it_does: A hard fork of zlib that reads and writes the same zlib, gzip and raw DEFLATE streams, with the same z_stream-style streaming API, one-shot compress/uncompress, gz* file functions and crc32/adler32. Built with ZLIB_COMPAT=ON it installs zlib.h and libz with zlib's API and ABI, so existing programs can relink or use LD_PRELOAD. The default native build instead exposes zlib-ng.h with zng_-prefixed functions, size_t lengths and uint32_t checksums, so it can sit next to the system zlib. The native API also adds zng_deflateSetParams, which can for example demand reproducible output.
how_it_is_fast: At first use, a runtime-filled function table (functable.c, using cpuid/hwcap) picks SIMD kernels for Adler32 (SSSE3 up to AVX512-VNNI, Neon dot-product), CRC32, compare256 match-length search, slide_hash and inflate's chunked match copy (chunkmemset). The CRC32 kernels are Intel's PCLMULQDQ/VPCLMULQDQ folding, a PMULL+EOR3 kernel from corsix/fast-crc32, and the Chorba algorithm (arXiv 2412.16398) for CPUs without carry-less multiply. Deflate swaps zlib's level-1 and level 3-6 match finders for Intel-derived strategies: deflate_quick (level 1 reads only the hash-chain head and emits static Huffman trees) and deflate_medium (levels 3-6). It also uses a 64K-entry Knuth multiplicative hash, and inflate adds a wider bit buffer and SIMD match copies.
when_to_use: Servers, log shippers or batch jobs that must emit standard gzip/zlib/DEFLATE at levels 1-9 and are bound by compression CPU: independent lzbench numbers show 2.2-2.5x zlib 1.3.1's compression throughput.
Speeding up an existing zlib-linked application or a whole distro without code changes: build with ZLIB_COMPAT=ON and relink or LD_PRELOAD. Fedora 40 adopted zlib-ng-compat as its system zlib.
Code that runs crc32()/adler32() over large buffers (gzip trailers, PNG, zip, framing) on x86-64 with PCLMULQDQ/AVX2/AVX-512 or on aarch64 with PMULL, where the SIMD kernel is picked at runtime.

One portable binary for many CPUs: runtime dispatch covers x86, ARM, POWER, RISC-V, LoongArch, MIPS and IBM Z (including DFLTCC hardware deflate), so a baseline x86-64 build still uses AVX-512 where the CPU has it.
Latency-sensitive callers that want every allocation to happen in deflateInit/inflateInit. zlib-ng allocates one block at init and can then only fail at init.
when_not_to_use: You control both ends and do not need DEFLATE. In the same lzbench run, zstd 1.5.6 -1 compresses 2.1x faster than zlib-ng -1 (422 vs 202 MB/s), gives a much better ratio (34.64% vs 44.41%) and decompresses 2.9x faster (1347 vs 471 MB/s).
Level 1 when output size matters. zlib-ng -1 output is about 22% larger than zlib -1 on Silesia (44.41% vs 36.45%), because deflate_quick uses static Huffman trees. Use level 2 or higher.

Maximum whole-buffer decompression speed: libdeflate 1.23 (not catalogued) decompresses Silesia at 860-919 MB/s against zlib-ng's 471-518 MB/s in the same lzbench table, but libdeflate has no streaming API.

Tests, caches or golden files that depend on zlib's exact compressed bytes or lengths. PORTING.md says the output differs from zlib, and Z_DEFLATE_REPRODUCIBLE only guarantees identical output within an identical zlib-ng build.

Apps that feed zlib a fixed pre-sized zalloc pool (the nginx pattern): zlib-ng needs more memory, about 350 KB for deflate and 42 KB for inflate on 64-bit, because inflate always allocates the full window. The README also warns against manually replacing the system libz.

integration.form: static lib or shared lib (CMake or configure build; vcpkg port)
integration.dependencies: none at runtime (libc only). Tests use Google Test and benchmarks use Google Benchmark, both optional build options.
integration.min_toolchain: C11 by default (CMake also accepts C99); CMake 3.14+ for 2.3.x; the project wiki recommends GCC 8.5+, Clang 11+ and MSVC 2022
integration.platforms: x86/x86-64 (SSE2 through AVX-512/VNNI/VPCLMULQDQ, runtime-detected), ARM/aarch64 (ARMv6, Neon, ARMv8 CRC/PMULL, EOR3), POWER8/9, RISC-V (RVV, Zbc), LoongArch (LSX/LASX), MIPS MSA and IBM Z (VX, DFLTCC), with generic C fallbacks. CI runs on Linux, macOS and Windows.
integration.thread_safety: Same model as zlib: separate streams can be used from separate threads if zalloc/zfree are thread-safe, but one stream must not be shared. The CPU-dispatch table is filled lazily with atomic pointer stores (__atomic on GCC/Clang, Interlocked on MSVC).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the ZLIB_COMPAT=ON build is API/ABI compatible with zlib (it advertises zlib 1.3.1, not 1.3.2) and can replace libz or be LD_PRELOADed. However, the compressed bytes differ from zlib's, it uses more memory, and the default native build needs zng_-prefixed calls and different types.

gotchas: The default CMake build is native mode (libz-ng, zlib-ng.h). You must pass ZLIB_COMPAT=ON to get a libz replacement. Linking a compat-mode zlib-ng into a process that also pulls in the system zlib through another library can crash or corrupt output (PORTING.md).

Skip 2.3.1: its Chorba CRC32 returned wrong CRCs for some inputs over 256 KB, which the 2.3.2 hotfix fixed. The latest release is 2.3.3 (Feb 2026). Newer work, such as PR #2353's inflate bit-refill change (about 13% faster inflate on Apple Silicon), exists only on the develop branch. Releases have lagged fixes before: the CVE-2022-37434 fix took about 7 months to ship.

MinGW-w64 GCC builds at -O0/-Og with AVX2/AVX-512 enabled crash in the chunkset code because of GCC PR54412 (misaligned vector spills); issue #1874 is still open. Workarounds are -O1 or higher, or -Wa,-muse-unaligned-vector-move.

Maintainers say zlib-ng uses a 4-byte minimum match where gzip allows 3, which can cost ratio on some binary data (#1922). A 2021 report (#947) found it slower than zlib on many tiny PNGs via LD_PRELOAD on a Raspberry Pi 4. The maintainers replied that zlib-ng is tuned for larger inputs.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick zlib-ng over zstd or LZ4 when the format must stay zlib/gzip/DEFLATE (HTTP gzip, PNG, zip, existing archives, readers you do not control) or when you want existing zlib callers to get faster with no code changes. If you control both ends, zstd -1 beats it on speed and ratio, and LZ4 decompresses about 8x faster (3716 vs 471 MB/s in lzbench) at a worse ratio.
verified_claims_summary: In the independent lzbench 2.0.1 table (gcc 14.2.0 with the Makefile's default -O3, one thread of an AMD EPYC 9554 at 3.10 GHz with turbo off, silesia.tar), zlib-ng 2.2.3 compressed 2.2x (-1), 2.5x (-6) and 2.4x (-9) faster than zlib 1.3.1 and decompressed 1.46-1.49x faster (471-518 vs 323-348 MB/s), with a much worse ratio at -1 and about equal ratios at -6 and -9. The README's '4x' only appears in the maintainers' own deflatebench runs (discussion #2022: 4.1-4.9x at level 6 on a Ryzen 8700GE and an i7-11700K, against a zlib develop build with unstated flags), and the CRC32/Adler32 speedups have no published numbers.
status_note: Actively developed (last commit 2026-09-25; latest release 2.3.3 on 2026-02-03) under the permissive Zlib license, OSS-Fuzz-tested, and accepted as Fedora 40's system-wide zlib replacement (zlib-ng-compat).
